```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE,
  fig.align = "center", dpi = 180, fig.pos = "H"
)
source("CreditLens.R", local = TRUE)
assets <- load_creditlens_assets(root = getwd())
invisible(list2env(assets$report$objects, envir = environment()))
chosen_cv <- cv[cv$family == lock$chosen, ]
chosen_test <- e$metrics[e$metrics$family == lock$chosen, ]
forest_test <- e$metrics[e$metrics$family == "forest", ]
baseline_test <- e$metrics[e$metrics$family == "baseline", ]
threshold <- e$thresholds[e$thresholds$family == lock$chosen, ]
cal <- e$calibration_numbers[e$calibration_numbers$family == lock$chosen, ]

f <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
}
n <- function(x) {
  format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
}
percent <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  paste0(f(100 * x, digits), "%")
}
table_report <- function(data, caption, digits = 3) {
  knitr::kable(
    data, caption = caption, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE,
    booktabs = TRUE, position = "H"
  )
}
report_figures <- lapply(assets$report$figures, function(bytes) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
  writeBin(bytes, path)
  normalizePath(path, winslash = "/")
})
```

# Introduction and data

CreditLens asks: **using information available at the end of six months of
credit-card history, how accurately can the recorded default-payment outcome
in the following month be predicted?** A probability, together with its
validation, helps students and analysts understand uncertainty and the
consequences of choosing a classification threshold.

The UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset describes Taiwanese customers
with April-September 2005 histories [1]. The downloaded Kaggle CSV contains
`r n(a$audit$rows)` customers, `r a$audit$columns` columns and
`r n(a$audit$events)` defaults (`r percent(a$audit$events / a$audit$rows, 2)`).
All 750,000 cell values were checked against the original UCI workbook.
Source URLs, file hashes and the comparison record are retained in the
accompanying asset file.

Each observation is one customer. All `r n(a$audit$unique_ids)` identifiers
are unique. No values are missing, no rows are exact duplicates and no
customers were excluded. The `r a$audit$duplicate_profiles` matching predictor
profiles across different identifiers remain separate customers. The outcome
is **0 = no recorded default payment; 1 = recorded default payment**
(internally No/Yes). It concerns the following month; the supplier does not
fully define its operational ascertainment. It is not assumed to be an annual
or regulatory default definition.

```{r candidates}
table_report(
  data.frame(
    Group = c("Credit limit", "Age", "Repayment status", "Bill statement", "Previous payment"),
    Variables = c("LIMIT_BAL", "AGE", "PAY_0, PAY_2-PAY_6", "BILL_AMT1-BILL_AMT6", "PAY_AMT1-PAY_AMT6"),
    Count = c(1, 1, 6, 6, 6),
    Unit = c("NT dollars", "years", "category", "NT dollars", "NT dollars")
  ),
  "Twenty original candidate predictors before selection.", digits = 0
)
```

The six monthly columns run from September, the most recent, back to April.
ID and outcome are excluded from predictors. Sex, education and marital status
are omitted to focus on payment history and financial information. This
choice does not establish fairness or remove every demographic proxy.

The development sample contains `r n(dev_n)` customers and
`r n(dev_events)` defaults. Mean age is
`r f(numeric_summary$mean[numeric_summary$variable == "AGE"], 1)` years
(SD `r f(numeric_summary$SD[numeric_summary$variable == "AGE"], 1)`). Median
credit limit is NT$`r n(numeric_summary$median[numeric_summary$variable == "LIMIT_BAL"])`
(IQR NT$`r n(numeric_summary$Q1[numeric_summary$variable == "LIMIT_BAL"])`-
`r n(numeric_summary$Q3[numeric_summary$variable == "LIMIT_BAL"])`). In this
sample, observed default proportions are
`r percent(status_summary$rate[status_summary$status == "0"])` for September
code 0 and `r percent(status_summary$rate[status_summary$status == "3+"])`
for 3+. These are descriptive associations, not causal effects or screening
criteria. The app supplies credit-limit distributions and status proportions
with sample counts and exact binomial intervals.

\newpage

# Methods: preparation and fitted procedures

All five approaches use the same 20 candidates and customers. Preparation is
fitted within the permitted training sample; no univariate significance
screening is performed. Complete data require no imputation. Missing required
app inputs are rejected explicitly.

Repayment codes are **nominal categories**, with -1 as reference. The expanded
published descriptions are -2 = no consumption, -1 = paid in full and
0 = use of revolving credit [2, 3]. The abbreviated UCI description uses
"paid duly" for -1 and omits -2 and 0. Revolving credit is not interpreted as
a precisely defined minimum payment. Codes -2, -1 and 0 remain distinct;
positive codes describe months of delay, with 3-9 grouped into 3+.

Within each training sample, code 1 is pooled into code 2 if fewer than 50
training observations have code 1. The final fitted mapping preserves
September code 1 and pools it for August-April. This predictor-only safeguard
followed a separating sparse category in an initial bootstrap pilot. All
200 final bootstrap replicates were restarted; stored checks established
identical outer/inner CV encodings under the revised rule. Complete-development
fits were regenerated before test evaluation. No holdout outcome chose the
mapping. This historical correction and its diagnostics are retained.

Monetary predictors use the fixed transformation
\(g(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)\log(1+|x|/1000)\), for raw NT-dollar amount
\(x\). It accommodates skewness, zeros and valid negative bills without
truncation. Age stays numerical. Factors use dummy terms for the linear models.

```{r specifications}
table_report(
  data.frame(
    Model = c("Full logistic", "LDA", "LASSO logistic", "Backward AIC", "Probability forest"),
    Specification = c(
      "Binomial logit; all 20 candidates; additive log-odds",
      "Empirical class priors; common covariance; scaled full-rank matrix",
      "Binomial glmnet; alpha = 1; retain penalized coefficients",
      "Full logistic start; backward AIC (k = 2); whole factors",
      "ranger; 500 trees; probability forest; ordered factor handling"
    )
  ),
  "Primary model specifications."
)
```

Logistic regression assumes additivity on the transformed log-odds scale.
Convergence, rank, finite coefficients and boundary probabilities are checked.
Full-model joint likelihood-ratio tests and IQR odds contrasts are descriptive
diagnostics; they do not select predictors. Odds ratios multiply odds, not
probabilities. LDA's class-conditional normality and common-covariance
assumptions are restrictive with these mixed categories and skewed histories
[4]. Training-only rank checks identify constant/dependent design columns.

For LASSO, preparation and standardization are repeated inside each inner
training fit. A decreasing, training-generated path of 100 penalties is
assessed by binomial deviance (twice log loss). The **one-SE rule** chooses
the largest penalty whose estimated loss is within one fold-based standard
error of the minimum [5]. Here SE is the SD of five fold losses divided by
\(\sqrt{5}\). This favors a stronger penalty and simpler fit within that
uncertainty allowance; it is separate from choosing the final model family.
The minimum-loss penalty is retained as a development sensitivity analysis.

The forest tunes mtry 4, 8 or 12 and minimum node size 10 or 30 by shared
inner-CV log loss; exact ties favor larger nodes, then lower mtry [6]. Its
final settings are `r spec$specification[spec$family == "forest"]`.
Out-of-bag error is supplementary and does not choose the final family.

\newpage

# Methods: validation, final choice and uncertainty

**Holdout validation.** Seed 5 reserves approximately 20% of each outcome
class: `r n(dev_n)` development and `r n(test_n)` test customers, with
`r n(dev_events)` and `r n(test_events)` defaults. IDs are disjoint.
Data-quality checks precede splitting. Detailed exploration, support ranges,
presets, tuning and model selection use development data only.

**Nested cross-validation.** Five stratified outer development folds are
shared by all families. Within each outer training sample, five shared inner
folds tune LASSO and the forest. Backward selection is repeated in every outer
training sample. Each development customer receives one outer-held-out
probability per family. All procedures are then fitted to complete development
data, using a separately saved five-fold allocation for final tuning. Split,
fold, seed and diagnostic records are retained. These are forms of internal
validation, not evidence of performance in a new time or population [4].

**Bootstrap validation and stability.** Seed 5005 generates 200 saved samples
of development customers with replacement. Every replicate refits preparation,
the full logistic starting model and backward AIC selection. It evaluates its
fitted pipeline on both the bootstrap sample and original development sample
[4]. With AUC denoted by \(C\), mean optimism and corrected apparent AUC are

\[
\widehat O=\frac{1}{200}\sum_{b=1}^{200}
(C_{b,\mathrm{boot}}-C_{b,\mathrm{original}}),
\qquad C_{\mathrm{corrected}}=C_{\mathrm{apparent}}-\widehat O.
\]

Original-variable inclusion frequencies describe **backward-AIC stability**,
not LASSO stability or causal importance. At 50% inclusion, 200 replicates
give Monte Carlo SE about 3.5 percentage points. The correction is reported
as a point estimate; percentiles of a fixed apparent AUC minus replicate
optimism do not capture full development uncertainty.

**Performance measures.** Log loss is the primary probability-quality measure:
it penalizes confident errors heavily. Brier score is mean squared probability
error. Lower is better for both. AUC measures default/non-default ranking,
counting ties as half-correct; higher is better. Probabilities are clipped to
[1e-15, 1-1e-15] only for logarithms. CV summaries pool outer-held-out
predictions; log loss equals the fold-size-weighted mean. A constant baseline
uses enclosing-training prevalence. Calibration plots compare probabilities
with observed rates in equal-count bins, with exact binomial intervals.

**Why LASSO was selected.** Before opening the holdout, the prespecified rule
identified the forest's minimum CV log loss,
`r f(min(lock$metrics$LogLoss), 4)`. Eligible families had loss no more than
1% above this and AUC no more than 0.01 below that family's AUC. LASSO
qualified: CV loss `r f(chosen_cv$LogLoss, 4)`, AUC `r f(chosen_cv$AUC, 4)`.
Among eligible families it required the fewest original inputs: **14**, versus
16 for backward AIC and 20 for full logistic and the forest. Remaining ties
would use lower loss, then the fixed order LASSO, backward, full, LDA, forest.
These are practical tolerances, not equivalence tests. Fewer required entries
and an inspectable additive log-odds structure motivated the trade-off;
fewer inputs do not automatically guarantee better generalization.

**Locked evaluation.** The selected family, fitted settings, required inputs
and model hashes were locked before test evaluation. Test AUC intervals and
one paired LASSO-versus-forest DeLong comparison condition on these fixed
fits [4, 7]; they omit variability from repeating development. Threshold 0.50
is prespecified, with flagging when probability is at least the threshold.
The app retains the development-fitted LASSO: no holdout tuning, recalibration,
threshold selection or development-plus-test refitting is performed.

\newpage

# Results: performance and threshold interpretation

```{r comparison}
comparison <- merge(
  e$metrics, cv[, c("family", "LogLoss")],
  by = "family", suffixes = c("_test", "_CV"), sort = FALSE
)
comparison <- comparison[match(c(families, "baseline"), comparison$family), ]
table_report(
  data.frame(
    Model = unname(model_labels[comparison$family]),
    Inputs = c(spec$original_inputs[match(families, spec$family)], 0),
    `CV loss` = f(comparison$LogLoss_CV, 4),
    `Test AUC (95% CI)` = sprintf(
      "%.4f (%.4f-%.4f)", comparison$AUC, comparison$Lower, comparison$Upper
    ),
    `Test loss` = f(comparison$LogLoss_test, 4),
    Brier = f(comparison$Brier, 4), check.names = FALSE
  ),
  paste0("Shared development CV and final holdout (", n(test_n), " customers).")
)
```

The forest subsequently performed better on the holdout across all three
reported measures: AUC `r f(forest_test$AUC, 4)` versus
`r f(chosen_test$AUC, 4)`, log loss `r f(forest_test$LogLoss, 4)` versus
`r f(chosen_test$LogLoss, 4)` and Brier `r f(forest_test$Brier, 4)` versus
`r f(chosen_test$Brier, 4)` for LASSO. The paired **forest-minus-LASSO AUC
advantage** is `r f(-e$paired$difference, 4)` (95% CI
`r f(-e$paired$CI[2], 4)`-`r f(-e$paired$CI[1], 4)`;
p = `r format.pval(e$paired$p, digits = 3)`). This supports a small ranking
advantage conditional on the trained fits. The models are not established
as statistically equivalent. LASSO remains implemented because of the
prespecified development-performance and input-count trade-off.

```{r roc-calibration, out.width='100%', fig.cap='Fixed-model holdout ROC and calibration. Calibration points show equal-count bins with exact binomial 95% intervals; axes span 0-1.'}
knitr::include_graphics(report_figures$roc_calibration, rel_path = FALSE)
```

LASSO ranks a random default/non-default pair correctly about
`r percent(chosen_test$AUC, 1)` of the time, counting ties as half-correct.
Its loss and Brier improve on the constant baseline
(`r f(baseline_test$LogLoss, 4)` and `r f(baseline_test$Brier, 4)`). Calibration
intercept is `r f(cal$Intercept)`, slope `r f(cal$Slope)` and offset intercept
`r f(cal$OffsetIntercept)` (ideal 0, 1 and 0). Point estimates near ideal
values and wide bin intervals do not establish perfect calibration; local
departures remain possible.

At threshold **0.50**, the LASSO gives **`r n(threshold$TP)` true positives,
`r n(threshold$FN)` missed defaults, `r n(threshold$FP)` false alarms and
`r n(threshold$TN)` true negatives**. It misses
`r n(threshold$FN)` of `r n(test_events)` observed defaults
(**`r percent(threshold$FN / test_events)`**). Sensitivity is
`r percent(threshold$Sensitivity)`, specificity
`r percent(threshold$Specificity)`, PPV `r percent(threshold$PPV)` and accuracy
`r percent(threshold$Accuracy)`. Lowering the threshold flags more customers,
increasing sensitivity while reducing specificity. High accuracy alone can
conceal many missed defaults in this imbalanced sample. These trade-offs
require decision costs and fresh validation before any operational policy.

\newpage

# Results: final model, importance and application

The final LASSO uses 14 original inputs: age, credit limit, six repayment
statuses and six previous payments. All six bill coefficients are zero.
There are `r length(model$selected_terms)` nonzero terms plus intercept, at
lambda `r f(model$settings$lambda, 9)`, without an unpenalized refit.
The intercept is `r f(model$settings$coefficients["(Intercept)"], 4)`;
September category coefficients relative to -1 (paid in full) are
`r f(model$settings$coefficients["PAY_01"], 4)` for 1,
`r f(model$settings$coefficients["PAY_02"], 4)` for 2 and
`r f(model$settings$coefficients["PAY_03+"], 4)` for 3+.
Coefficients add on the log-odds scale. The full nonzero table, intercept,
references and transformations are supplied in the asset file and app.
No ordinary unpenalized p-values are attached to selected coefficients.

```{r importance}
top <- head(importance, 4)
table_report(
  data.frame(
    Input = top$variable,
    `CV permutation loss increase` = f(top$increase, 4),
    `Backward inclusion (%)` = f(
      100 * stability$frequency[match(top$variable, stability$variable)], 1
    ), check.names = FALSE
  ),
  "LASSO-procedure importance and separate backward-AIC stability."
)
```

Permutation importance averages the increase in outer-held-out log loss
after shuffling an original input, using three repetitions per fold. It
describes the **selected LASSO procedure**: outer-fold fits can retain
different variables from the deployed complete-development fit. Correlated
histories can share predictive information. Backward inclusion frequencies
come from a different procedure and do not measure LASSO selection stability.
Backward apparent AUC `r f(boot$apparent_AUC, 4)` minus mean optimism
`r f(boot$mean_optimism, 4)` yields `r f(boot$corrected_AUC, 4)` (200 successful
replicates; zero failures). This is slightly above backward outer-CV AUC
`r f(cv$AUC[cv$family == "backward"], 4)`; the assessments use different
training samples and correction procedures. Neither replaces the holdout.

Repayment effects are not constrained to increase. In the saved higher
preset, holding everything else fixed, September codes 1, 2 and 3+ give
`r paste(percent(repayment_sensitivity$probability), collapse = ", ")`,
respectively. Sparse severe-delay groups, correlated histories and
unconstrained nominal effects can produce this pattern. It is not by itself
a programming error, and coefficients were not manually altered. Profile
changes describe predictions, not causal intervention effects.

The three-page app explains the data, makes frozen-model predictions and
explores holdout performance. It highlights 14 active inputs, collapses the
excluded bill candidates, and compares saved A with current B in percentage
points alongside changed inputs. Lower, middle and higher presets give
9.5%, 15.5% and 53.0%; lower-to-higher is +43.5 percentage points. Required
input edits clear stale results. Validation, reset, safe preset loading and
extrapolation notices support interpretation. The performance page shows
missed defaults, false alarms and a threshold marker on ROC; AUC, loss and
Brier stay fixed as the threshold changes. PPV is undefined if nobody is flagged.

```{r app-view, out.width='55%', fig.cap='Predicted probability and saved-scenario comparison in CreditLens.'}
if (!is.null(report_figures$app_predict)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(report_figures$app_predict, rel_path = FALSE)
}
```

Public application: [pimvdb.shinyapps.io/creditlens](`r deployment$url`).
App and report use release **`r identity$release_id`**, model
**`r substr(identity$model_id, 1, 12)`**.

\newpage

# Discussion and conclusions

CreditLens implements a complete workflow: five model families, shared nested
cross-validation, a reserved holdout and a 200-replicate backward-procedure
bootstrap. The selected LASSO balances development probability performance
with fewer required inputs and an inspectable additive structure. It does
not have the best holdout performance: the forest performs better in ranking,
log loss and Brier score. Keeping the original choice preserves the stated
performance-simplicity decision instead of selecting again using test outcomes.

LASSO offers useful, imperfect discrimination and better probability quality
than predicting prevalence for everyone. Calibration needs separate scrutiny;
near-ideal point estimates are insufficient evidence of accurate probabilities
throughout the risk range. At 0.50, high specificity coexists with missing
about 69% of defaults. Users should therefore consider sensitivity, specificity,
predictive value and the costs of errors together, rather than accuracy alone.
Moving a threshold in the app illustrates this trade-off; it does not discover
a validated lending policy.

Strengths include verified source data, no unnecessary imputation, retention
of valid extreme and negative amounts, shared evaluation samples,
training-only preparation and tuning, repetition of backward selection inside
resampling, and a family lock preceding test evaluation. Stored fitted assets
and shared prediction functions connect the report to the app. Supporting
records distinguish CV importance, backward stability and final coefficients.

Limitations concern both data and modeling. The historical Taiwanese cohort
does not establish performance in contemporary banking or another country.
The supplier-specific outcome is incompletely defined. Grouped categories and
fixed monetary transformations simplify measurement. Additive log-odds and
LDA assumptions restrict the linear approaches; the forest grid is finite.
Sparse severe delays and correlated monthly histories affect coefficients,
selection and importance, including the non-monotonic category example.
Penalized coefficients are predictive associations, not causal estimates.
Omitting demographic fields does not establish fairness. Conditional holdout
intervals omit variability from a new split, tuning and model-family selection.

Further work should use temporal or geographic validation, clearer outcome
ascertainment, subgroup calibration checks and explicit decision costs.
Recalibration, if needed for a new population, would require separate
development and evaluation data. The current app is useful for teaching and
communicating prediction models; its evidence does not support present-day
automated credit decisions.
